experiments.full_name: Burning and Suppression of Solids II
experiments.platform: International Space Station, Microgravity Science Glovebox (per NTRS abstract)

principal_investigators.note: Surnames as given in the PI column of the table; test counts: Bhattacharjee 22, Ferkul 4, Fernandez-Pello 27, Miller 20, Olson 27, T'ien 29

experiments.description: Second phase of the Burning and Suppression of Solids investigation. Flames on solid fuels were burned in a small wind tunnel in microgravity. Samples include thin and thick flat samples, acrylic (PMMA) slabs and rods, spheres and cylinders; this table also lists Nomex, SIBAL, SIBAL-type and candle (wax) samples.
objectives: Improve spacecraft fire safety and the understanding of how combustion behaves in space, so fires can be avoided.

Learn how airflow speed, fuel thickness, preheating of the fuel and oxygen concentration change flame appearance, growth, spread and extinction, in both opposed-flow and concurrent-flow configurations.
Support selection of the safest spacecraft materials and better fire-fighting methods for future missions.

documented_results.finding: Flames were found to be very sensitive to airflow in the 0-5 cm/s range.
At very low airflow (below roughly 1 cm/s) flames persisted as dim, steady blue flames. These are less hazardous, but a sudden rise in airflow can make them flare up quickly.

The paper reports well over 100 tests across BASS and BASS-II combined, covering different sample shapes, flow speeds and oxygen levels. It covers both phases, so some findings may stem from PSI-26 runs.

experiments.description: A continuing series of droplet-combustion experiments in which methanol and heptane droplets are burned in microgravity under varied ambient pressure and oxygen / nitrogen / CO2 / helium mixtures. The table lists one row per test with ambient composition, droplet diameter, flame extinction diameter, burning rate, burn time and how the test ended.
objectives: Document the FLEX droplet-combustion data and methods for the scientific community (stated aim of the NTRS data report).
Test fuels and environmental conditions that mimic real combustor conditions (LabXchange FLEX-2 description); topics include flame extinguishment and spacecraft fire safety.

documented_results.finding: The NTRS data report presents results of the first 284 tests, run between March 2009 and December 2011, together with hardware, diagnostics, procedures and analysis methods. Its abstract does not summarise scientific outcomes, so none are listed here.

experiments.platform: Remotely operated module (about 1 m x 1.5 m) on the Cygnus OA-6 cargo spacecraft, run after undocking from the ISS

principal_investigators.note: Not given in the table. The NTRS paper is by Ferkul et al.

experiments.description: A large-scale fire test in an unoccupied spacecraft: a sheet of SIBAL fabric (fiberglass-cotton blend) was burned in a flow duct, once with the flame spreading in the same direction as the airflow (concurrent) and once against it (opposed), at an average 20 cm/s airflow. Two cameras recorded each burn.
objectives: Observe fire growth and spread in microgravity at a much larger scale than earlier experiments.
Check whether NASA's material flammability selection methods reliably predict behaviour in low gravity.
Measure how microgravity and reduced oxygen affect flame size.

documented_results.finding: The sample was about ten times larger than any previous microgravity fire test.
In the concurrent test the flame stayed limited in size, whereas a similar upward-spreading flame on Earth would accelerate and grow.
Flame spread was slower in this large tunnel than in smaller microgravity tunnels; the authors attribute this to flow acceleration from hot-gas expansion in small tunnels.
The burn used up a notable share of the available oxygen (the abstract gives no usable unit).
Conclusion: forced flow in microgravity gives distinct flame behaviour that depends on experiment scale, so full-scale tests matter for spacecraft fire safety.

experiments.description: Overheated spacecraft materials were used to generate smoke, and the size and distribution of the smoke particles were measured, together with how particles change as the smoke ages. The reported campaign used 30 samples (six each of five materials) at different airflow rates, heating temperatures and aging times. This table lists only 8 samples, with values for the four Teflon samples.
objectives: Measure the size and distribution of smoke particles from materials found on spacecraft.
Evaluate the ionization smoke detectors used on the Space Shuttle and the photoelectric detectors used on the ISS.
Gather data for predicting smoke particle growth and for testing future detection technologies.

documented_results.finding: Teflon smoke was mostly made of particles smaller than 1 micron, yet a large share of the total aerosol mass sat in particles larger than 1 micron.
Aging mainly made particles coagulate, with few lost to walls: particle counts fell sharply while total mass stayed roughly constant.
Average diameters were around 100-200 nm but can mislead: silicone smoke averaged 227 nm while almost half its mass was in particles over 1000 nm.
Ionization detectors respond well to the abundant sub-micron particles, and light-scattering detectors performed well in most cases.
Overheating before a fire gives broader size distributions, so detectors covering a wider size range may be more reliable; detection should target early pyrolysis products rather than soot.
